newsitem.title: USA: Cohen begins first Pacific-Asia trip on Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Cohen begins first Pacific-Asia trip on Saturday.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen leaves on Saturday on a week-long trip to the Pacific and Asia to meet U.S. troops and discuss security in that region with leaders of Japan and South Korea.

High on Cohen's agenda for talks with military commanders and the allies is the stabilising presence of U.S. troops, the volatile situation in communist North Korea and the growth of China as an economic and military force.

He is also expected to take up bilateral issues ranging from the controversial presence of American troops on the Japanese island of Okinawa to South Korea's consideration of whether to buy Russian SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles.

A senor U.S. defence official told reporters in advance of the secretary's first trip to the Pacific that Cohen would assure Tokyo and Seoul that Washington plans to keep 100,000 troops in the Pacific and Asia for the forseeable future.

Some 47,000 are in Japan - over half on Okinawa -- and 36,000 in South Korea. The Pentagon is examining military strategy and deployments in light of budget cuts, and some Asian nations worry the Pacific presence might be reduced.

"I think you can safely say that, from top to bottom, the U.S. government supports the continuing forward deployment of about 100,000 (troops) in the Asia-Pacific region," said the senior defence official, who asked not to be identified.

Cohen will go first to Hawaii on Saturday for talks with Adm. Joseph Prueher, commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific. He will be in Japan on Monday and Tuesday and go to Korea for two days before flying back to Washington on Friday.
He arrives in Japan at a critical time for the U.S. military there.

Cohen will meet defence and foreign policy leaders in Tokyo and may confer with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who is pushing legislation to force landowners, including those on Okinawa, to continue leasing land for U.S. bases.

In September 1995, the widely publicised rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen triggered a public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence on the island and prompted an official review.
Many Okinawans remain opposed to the U.S. presence despite an agreement to reduce artillery fire and aircraft noise and other efforts to make it less intrusive.

The situation is complicated by a new inquiry into a possible assault by a U.S. sailor against a Japanese woman at Yokosuka naval base, although that incident has apparently not sparked much reaction in Japan.

The sailor, at the U.S. military headquarters at Yokosuka, is being held on suspicion of sexually assaulting and beating up his Japanese girlfriend. Japanese media have reported the incident as a violent quarrel between lovers and not a rape or sexual assault, based on police assessments.

In Japan, the Pentagon official told Reuters, Cohen will also discuss with Defence Minister Fumio Kyuma and others Japan's continued internal debate on how it might cooperate with the United States on an anti-missile defence inititive.
In South Korea, Cohen will meet President Kim Young-sam, Defence Minister Kim Dong-jin and Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha.

He will also visit U.S. and South Korean troops in the Demilitarized Zone between North and South Korea and will hold talks with Gen. John Tilelli, the U.S. commander in Korea. Tilelli told Congress last month that he was worried about the volatile situation in North Korea, which has 1.1 million troops and is thought to have chemical and biological weapons.

North Korea has tentatively agreed to four-way peace talks with South Korea, the United States and China, but many in Seoul and Washington fear hunger and the collapse of the North Korean economy could cause Pyongyang to lash out at the South.
